analysis.one_liner: Restores minimum prevailing wages for construction workers on federal Katrina rebuilding contracts.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by 205 cosponsors, was referred to committee in September 2005 and never received a vote before that Congress ended in January 2007.
analysis.plain_summary: After Hurricane Katrina, President Bush suspended the Davis-Bacon Act, a rule requiring contractors on federally funded construction to pay workers the local prevailing wage. This bill would cancel that suspension in the Katrina disaster area, so workers rebuilding the Gulf Coast on federal contracts would get paid the standard local wage again. The bill was introduced on September 14, 2005, sent to the House Education and Workforce Committee, then sent to a subcommittee, and never came up for a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Construction workers in Louisiana, Mississippi, and Alabama who would rebuild hurricane-damaged areas under federal contracts. The Davis-Bacon wage rules would require their employers to pay the prevailing local wage, which is typically well above what federal contractors were paying after the suspension.

how_it_helps.text: The bill reinstates the Davis-Bacon Act's wage requirements on all federal contracts in the counties affected by Hurricane Katrina, overriding the President's September 8, 2005 suspension proclamation.
It applies to contracts entered into on or after the bill's enactment, so new federal rebuilding contracts would have to pay prevailing wages again.
The affected areas include counties in Louisiana, Mississippi, and Alabama listed in the President's Katrina proclamation.

analysis.who_pays: Federal contractors doing Katrina rebuilding work, who would face higher labor costs than under the suspended rules, and to a lesser degree the federal taxpayer if contract bids rise to cover those wages.

drawbacks.text: Prevailing wage rules raise the labor cost of federally funded construction, which means each federal rebuilding dollar buys less; supporters of the suspension argued that lower wages would stretch disaster money further and speed rebuilding.
Davis-Bacon compliance involves paperwork and wage determination processes that can slow contract awards, a real concern during an emergency recovery effort.
The bill only covered counties in the President's Katrina proclamation, leaving workers on other disaster cleanups without the same protection.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core tradeoff is straightforward: prevailing wage requirements mean Gulf construction workers get paid a standard local wage on federally funded rebuilding, while the government pays more per contract. For workers displaced by the storm, the wage floor mattered directly; critics' argument that suspending it sped up rebuilding was contested at the time and the bill's narrow scope (Katrina counties only) limited both its cost and its reach.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the House Education and Workforce Committee, then sent to its subcommittee a month later, and it never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before that Congress ended in January 2007.

narrative.text: President Bush's September 8, 2005 proclamation suspended the Davis-Bacon prevailing wage requirements for federal contracts in Hurricane Katrina-affected areas, which this bill was written to overturn.
Rep. George Miller introduced the bill on September 14, 2005, with 205 cosponsors: 203 Democrats, 1 Independent, and 1 Republican.
The House referred the bill to the Education and Workforce Committee the day it was introduced.
On October 12, 2005, the bill was referred to the Subcommittee on Workforce Protections, and the congressional record shows no further action — no hearing, no committee vote, no floor vote.
The 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007, and the bill died in committee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Federal contractors doing Gulf Coast rebuilding work came out ahead: the wage suspension stayed in effect for the duration of the reconstruction, keeping their labor costs below prevailing-wage levels. The Gulf Coast construction workers the bill was written to protect never got the wage floor.

for.name: Rep. George Miller
for.role: House Education and Workforce Committee member; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on September 14, 2005 to reinstate Davis-Bacon wages in Katrina-affected counties.

for.name: 205 House cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors — 203 Democrats, 1 Independent (Bernie Sanders), and 1 Republican (Rep. Vic Snyder).

against.name: President George W. Bush
against.what_they_did: Issued the September 8, 2005 proclamation suspending Davis-Bacon wage requirements for federal Katrina contracts, the action this bill sought to reverse; the suspension remained in place.

against.name: Rep. John Boehner
against.role: Chair, House Education and Workforce Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a committee markup or hearing; the record shows only referral to committee and then to a subcommittee.

against.name: House Republican leadership
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the House floor; no vote was ever scheduled in the 109th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Support was overwhelmingly Democratic — 203 of the 205 cosponsors were Democrats, joined by one Independent and one Republican — while the committee chaired by a Republican that controlled the agenda never acted on it.

industries.note: The bill would have required contractors on federally funded Katrina rebuilding to pay prevailing wages, raising their labor costs. The suspension staying in effect kept their costs down — the direct tradeoff against workers' paychecks.
The bill's beneficiaries: workers rebuilding hurricane-damaged areas on federal contracts would have been guaranteed the local prevailing wage. The bill's failure left them without it.
